speechtext:
May we have an explanation
from the mover and seconder of this motion?

This bill appears in
my name and the case is a very simple one.

Procedure Respecting Divorce
The evidence can be read in about five
minutes by any hon. member. One of my hon. friends opposite asks me to explain the bill. He has before him the evidence taken before the senate committee and I think he will agree with me that this is a bill which should get its second reading and be referred to the committee on miscellaneous private bills.
Briefly, I may say for the information of my hon. friend, the petitioner is a well known physician and surgeon in a city in the province of Ontario. The respondent did not appear before the senate committee. The petitioner and the respondent were married in the city of Kingston on January 1, 1923 and the respondent was married in Lima, Ohio on October 8, 1928. As I say, the respondent did not appear before the senate committee, but the man whom she married in Lima, Ohio, was present and gave evidence. The case is not complicated; it is very simple. I am not a lawyer, but I see no room for argument over this bill. Let me say that the fact that I sponsor this bill is no indication of my attitude towards the principle of divorce. I do not consider that the principle of divorce is in question at all at the moment. As for that principle I yield to no hon. member in this house my sincere conviction, although I will not now state what it is-but will do so if the opportunity ever warrants it; I voted against the bill from the senate for a divorce court in Ontario because I thought that public sentiment in the province of Ontario did not demand the establishment of such a court. The only method which we have of granting divorces is therefore the procedure which we are following this afternoon. Whether divorce is right or wrong is apart from the question. I deplore the fact that there are SO1 many applications in Ontario, but at the same time we are bound to deal with them and this is the only machinery we have for the purpose. I would therefore ask the house to give the bill its second reading.

I note that the
senate committee on divorce, in making their report, say that the requirements of the rules of the senate have been complied with in all material respects. Will the mover of the resolution give the house some idea of the requirements of the rules of the senate?

No hon. gentleman
knows the requirements better than does my hon. friend, and I do not propose to enter into any argument with him.
Mr. A. E. RO'SS (Kingston City): This is the bill m regard to which it was my purpose

to say something but I understand that the evidence given will not be considered until the bill is in committee. My point is this. I believe that the house should now consider whether the requirements at present demanded for the obtaining of divorce are satisfactory. I have nothing to say on the question of divorce, but this country recognizes divorce as does the country across the line. We pay mutual respect to marriages in the two countries, and when a couple have been legitimately divorced and legitimately and legally married, then I think the question should be raised now as to whether that condition should or should not be called adultery. At present we hurl from each side of the line the epithet, at people legitimately married, that they are living in a state of adultery. This question I intend to bring up in connection with this bill in committee of the whole.

I must thank the
promoter of the bill for having given an outline of the case. It is a distinct improvement on the procedure we have had in the past. However, I would say that the question I asked has a direct bearing on the case. As yet it has not been explained to me just what are the requirements of the senate; I do not think we know exactly on what we are voting. I have been in the house some eight sessions. When a member first comes here I imagine he takes these bills as matters of routine, but as the years go on some of us begin to inquire with regard to the principles involved and I confess frankly that I do not know exactly under what rules the senate works in these matters. If I am not mistaken-and I speak subject to correction by the lawyers present- we have no statutory arrangements with regard to divorce, hence we hardly know just where we are.
I have heard it stated in this house that there is only one ground for divorce, but that is not correct; to my knowledge divorce has been granted in this house on other grounds than that of adultery, and as far as the powers of this house are concerned, I see no reason why wider grounds should not be recognized. Personally I am inclined to think that there is a danger in over-emphasizing the mere physical act of adultery in making it the only ground for divorce. The other day I came across an interesting statement in the Life and Letters of the Earl of Birkenhead;
It must be admitted 'by all the right-minded people that the duties of chastity and continence shall be insisted upon. But so to limit the causes of divorce is to ignore the fact that the spiritual and moral aspects of marriage are incomparably more important than the physical side.

Procedure Respecting Divorce
And again:
It is not to the public welfare that utter unsuitability for the marriage state whether the cause be moral, mental or physical, should not involve the same consequences.
That is the considered opinion of one of the most eminent British jurists, so I do not think we can sweep away all arguments of that kind and maintain that divorce can be granted only on one ground.
Further than that, much of this evidence would not be received in a court of law. Since these discussions began I have read a number of the cases and I find very often that the fact that the parties registered at the same hotel is considered evidence of improper relationship. I can quite readily understand that anyone desirous of securing a divorce could easily arrange a frame-up under such circumstances, and collusion might be very common. We have no information before us with regard to a situation of this character. Before speaking on the principle of the bill, may I, in order to clear up any misunderstanding there may be as to the powers of this parliament in legislative and judicial matters, read paragraph 844 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms:
The proceedings of parliament in passing private bills partake of both a judicial and legislative character. The promoters of the bill appear as suitors while those who apprehend injury tare admitted as adverse parties to the suit. The former may prove that their own interests will be advanced by the success of the bill and no one may urge any objection; yet. if the house apprehends that the bill will be hurtful to the community, it may be rejected.
I would not undertake to define exactly what constitutes a bill of divorce, but in view of the fact that to-day we have on the order paper seventy-seven divorce bills, I think the matter is of sufficient importance to warrant our careful consideration. What would happen if we had seventy-seven railway bills, or seventy-seven patent bills, or the same number of any other kind of private bills? We would not pass them as a mere matter of form. Yet these divorce bills strike at the very root of the nation, at the family itself. A former minister of justice, the Hon. Mr. Doherty, who occupied that office in the late Conservative government, defines a bill of divorce in these words:
An act that grants a divorce is a private act, like any other private act. The house as well as the senate must enact it. The parties
come here asking for it, just as they come with other private bills when they want to get something that the general law of the country does not give them. And it is precisely because the general law of the country says: once you are married you can never marry again while your consort is alive, that when one wants to be relieved of the operation of that general law, he comes to the parliament of Canada and asks for a law for himself; and each one of these petitioners goes away, where he succeeds, carrying with him a law that is a law for him -a law that takes him out of the operation of the general law.
This view is also shared by the Hon. Mr. Nickle, a former distinguished member of this house, who on one occasion introduced a divorce bill, and after a long discussion it was passed, but it failed in the senate. At the time Mr. Nickle said:
It is well known to every member that any person who has the means and cares to present a petition to parliament if he is in a position to demonstrate that adultery has been committed has a moral right to divorce, but in Ontario and Quebec, because we have no divorce courts, there is no legal right to divorce.

Does not my hon. friend agree that there is no general divorce law either in Ontario or in Quebec? Therefore, so far as those provinces are concerned, there is no forum except parliament before which parties seeking a divorce may appear.
Divorce is not recognized either in Ontario or in Quebec.
There is no divorce court in either province; that is the point.

I do not want to quote again the views of Sir Hector Langevin which I gave to the house last week, but he was solicitor general when the British North America Act was passed, and he said then that they were not introducing the principle of divorce either in Ontario or in Quebec. However, they found divorce courts already established in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and therefore the matter had to be taken into consideration with regard to the other two provinces. The fathers of confederation were wise men. They decided not to establish divorce courts in Ontario and Quebec, but to place the power of granting divorce in the jurisdiction of the federal parliament, and in this way make it more difficult to secure a divorce; for they were of opinion that it would not be in the interest of the country to facilitate the granting of divorce. Their wisdom was proved by the fact that in the following ten years only seven applications for divorce were granted by parliament. Last year there were 785 divorces. I am glad that there are two provinces in

Procedure Respecting Divorce
this Dominion with an admirable record in matters of divorce-Prince Edward Island and Quebec. I respect the views of every member of this house. The people of the west may have different ideas on the subject. The Divorce Act, passed in 1857, has been applied to the western country. At the time that the member for West Calgary introduced the measure before the house with regard to Alberta and Saskatchewan, it was argued that the hearing of these cases by the courts would reduce the number of applications for divorce; but the very contrary has happened. And if we establish divorce courts in Ontario and Quebec the same thing would happen. The people of these two provinces have a right to divorce courts if they so decide, but up to the present they have decided that they do not want such courts. Neither province has yet asked for the establishment of divorce courts. I question very much, even if we had passed the bill recently introduced to establish a divorce court in Ontario, whether we would have been acting within our powers, for the British North America Act, as has been said repeatedly, is a contract between the various provinces, and the consent of the Ontario legislature would have to be secured before we could impose a divorce court on the province.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we have agreed not to discuss the evidence in this or any other case at the present stage, for the very good reason that that evidence is not yet before us, not yet having been dealt with by the private bills committee of this house. In the old days nine senators were required to form the senate divorce committee, but to-day I notice that that committee is composed of only five members. I do not know whether they have to be unanimous or whether a bare majority could accept the evidence adduced before them as being sufficient to warrant a divorce; but in the latter event we would have three senators reporting in favour of a divorce bill their report of course being accepted by the senate, and then in turn this would be automatically accepted by the private bills committee of this house if we followed the usual practice. To this we object. The member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) objects on another ground: he desires to have these cases sent to a divorce court to be set up in Ontario. I object to divorce on the ground that marriage is sacred, that it is a contract for life and cannot be dissolved except by the death of one of the parties. That was the view in England for eighteen hundred years until the passing of the Divorce Act in 1857. But before that time the matrimonial courts annulled marriage for certain reasons. In Quebec we 
have what are known as judicial separations. Under this procedure husband and wife may separate, and ait the same time fair and reasonable provision may be made for alimony and for the custody of the children. We cannot do that; all we can do is to grant a divorce. By so doing we throw the children out on the street and put the guilty party on the same footing as the innocent. So we are establishing in effect the principle of polygamy, for a man may secure a divorce this year, marry again, and next year apply for another divorce, and, that having been granted, marry again, and continue this course indefinitely.

speechtext: But the hon. member will not deny that in any of the provinces the courts are there for the purpose of giving redress.

That may be an argument in favour of sending it to the courts. But at the present time the principal reason why these divorces are becoming so numerous is that there are certain classes of people who get married to-day with the idea that if matters do not go as they expect they can always resort to a divorce court, and if that is not effective in the province in which they reside they can come to parliament, believing that in doing so they automatically obtain a divorce. When they come here they ask a favour; it is a law of exception in this case, because there is no divorce law in either Ontario or Quebec.
I do not wish to delay the house, Mr. Speaker, when the majority have declared in favour of divorce, but I think it my duty to show the grave responsibility which parliament assumes in allowing this state of things to continue. I should like to cite a few words to indicate what has taken place in the United States. Let me quote the Rev. Dr. Gwynne on Divorce in America undter State and Church. This reverend gentleman is secretary of an association in the United1 States whose object it is to preserve among all peoples, irrespective of creed and race, respect for the sanctity of marriage. This bodty is known as the Sanctity of Marriage Association. I quote:
Let us now look at some results of this anarchic condition of our legislation, as they are seen in the official reports of the Bureau

That is what divorce is accomplishing. There was a time when divorce was practically non-existent in this country, but it exists to-day, and if it continues it will be ten times worse ten years from now. In my opinion therefore we should call a halt; divorce should not be granted by parliament at all. In the provinces where divorce is granted the matter is largely one of provincial rights, civil rights being within the province; the solemnization [DOT]of marriage comes within the purview of the province. For these reasons I can add only one more objection to the principle of divorce and declare that I will oppose it as strenuously as I can every time the opportunity presents itself.
One point is raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) as to increasing the grounds on which divorce may be granted, and not confining it simply to adultery. I do not know why in Canada the cause has been limited to adultery; I do not know on what ground we proceed, whether it is the practice in England. But I find in this book of the Rev. Dr. Gwynne, with an introduction by Doctor Manning, quotations from the Bible which I do not care to read now seeing that they are familiar to all hon. members of this house-quotations from St. Matthew, St. Mark, St. Luke, and verbatim utterances from our Lord and Saviour; and there is absolutely nothing in all these references which authorizes the remarriage of divorced persons. There is no authority in the Bible for it. So that on what ground divorce has been limited here to the single cause of adultery I fail to see. If we were to follow the suggestion made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre we might adopt the practice of the United States. There is only one state in the American Union which has never established a divorce court, and that is South Carolina; but in the other states they have as many as fifty-two different causes for divorce.
A man is divorced in one state and is married in another, and so on, and altogether there is a most chaotic state of confusion. For many years in the United States a strong effort has been made for the limitation to the federal authorities of the granting of divorce, in order to stem the ravages of the evil. I will say no more, and I hope that more of us who are conscientiously opposed to divorce, and who realize its ravages, will take the opportunity when it arises to voice their opinion, because they know in their inmost hearts that divorce in Canada has reached the stage where it has become a real and a grave problem.

I was in hopes that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) would give an answer to the question asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth).
I believe that everyone in the house agrees that the question now before us is one of great importance; it is important not only to the individuals who may be concerned in the bills before parliament, but from the point of view of parliament itself; and it is also important to the general public. We were told by the sponsor of this bill that the people of Ontario were not ready for divorce courts.
I might reply with equal confidence and authority and tell the hon. gentleman that the people of Canada are not yet ready for the kind of thing we are doing; and if the people of Ontario are refusing to have divorce courts then I as a member of this house am prepared to refuse to follow the present course. Then where does my hon. friend get? I hope the seriousness of the question will induce the Prime Minister or some other member of the government to indicate to the house some reasonable way out. I would suggest that we either, first of all, drop all divorce cases; or secondly that we take them seriously, considering them as they ought to be considered, in a dignified manner, and enlarging the powers of parliament to deal with all phases of divorce, giving authority to the senate committee to look after the children of divoroed people, and also the power to deal separately with the eases which may come before the committee, from the point of view of remarriage and on the basis of the merits of each individual case; or, in the third place, if we do not do that, that we proceed as early as possible to refer the matter to the proper courts to deal with. Now, what course shall we pursue?

Order. A point of order has been raised.

A good deal of this debate has evidently been out of order. There is a rule of the house which provides distinctly that questions arising in a previous debate in the same session may not be referred to. In this house a bill has been introduced and carried forward to second reading, and which was passed by another house of this parliament, providing for the establishment of a divorce court in Ontario. The whole subject matter of many of the speeches of hon. members who, shall I say, are delaying this house, has consisted in the fact that they are offended by the action of this parliament, to which they should be subject. We have passed upon this matter for this session at least, and any hon. member speaking to any divorce bill before this parliament, either now or during the rest of this session, should be confined strictly to the merits or demerits of the particular case which he is discussing.

I have no objection to the
remarks of my hon. friend; I am glad to note that they do not apply to me. I am just about to conclude my remarks by asking that the Prime Minister or some member of the government respond to the urgent appeal of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), not only in respect to the present bill before the house but in respect to other bills of the same character which will come before the house later. I have pointed out the courses open to this parliament, as I see them. I do not suppose any hon. member wishes to be associated with the present way of doing this kind of business. If the bill we are now considering goes to the private bills committee, where we may obtain information which will enable us to pass the bill in committee and send it back to the house-

The point of order raised by the hon. member is well taken in principle; when the house has passed judgment on a question that question cannot foe revived during the same session, but may be revived at another session. However, as I stated the other day, various divorce bills have been introduced, one of which is now before the house; some hon. members are in favour of these bills while others oppose them, as is their right, and it is rather difficult to deter-
mine the difference between the general principle of whether or not a divorce court should be established and the point at issue. It is all the same question and I cannot prevent the speakers who oppose these particular divorce bills from bringing up their objections against the principle of divorce itself. However, it is easy for so able a parliamentarian as the hon. member now speaking to confine his remarks as much as possible to the bill presently before the house.

I shall endeavour so to
do; my only reference to the matter to which Your Honour alludes was made in reply to the statement of the sponsor of the bill. I am sorry he was so sadly out of order and I am sorry I followed him in that regard.
I turn again to the Prime Minister in the hope that he will show us some way out of the dilemma, because it must be clear to every hon. member of the house that if we are seriously to consider the three hundred divorce bills which will come before us, we must either sit continuously or not do the work very well. I believe the Prime Minister must agree that this matter of divorce has become too great a task for this parliament to undertake. It is one /thing for parliament to have the constitutional right to grant a divorce or a separation when such a thing occurs once a year or something like that, but it is another thing for parliament to consider three hundred of these bills each year together with all the other things to which we must give our attention. That is the situation which has developed during recent years, and that is the situation to which I hope the Prime Minister will address himself now.

That I may be in order I would make it clear that I am simply seeking to answer a question relating largely to procedure. I gather that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) is of the view that by this time the government should see that this method of dealing with divorce bills is anything but satisfactory, or in other words that under the present method it is within the power of a few members of this house to block the entire business of parliament, if they so desire, in order to demonstrate their dissatisfaction with the prevailing system of granting divorces through the agency of private bills.
I must confess that up to the present time I have not been able to see a way of dealing with these matters other than by a divorce court on the one hand or by private bills on the other. As my hon. friend is

Procedure Respecting Divorce
aware, during the present session this house decided against a divorce court for the prov-ince#of Ontario, and that method cannot he considered again at this time. Until some other method suggests itself I fail to see a better way of dealing with the situation than that which has prevailed heretofore. I think the discussion which has taken place so far and what has been demonstrated as to the amount of time which will be consumed if all individual bills for divorce are to be considered in this house, have made it evident that some method other than that at present in force should be followed, but I would remind hon. gentlemen that the matter is not one to be solved in a moment or by the stroke of a pen. I will say to hon. members of the house that the government will continue as we have been doing to give very serious thought to this question; I could not promise that we will find a solution during this session of parliament, but I would express the hope that by another session, by conference in the interval with members of the house and by other methods, we may find it possible to effect some arrangement which will enable those seeking divorce to secure such redress as should be given them by a means which will commend itself more completely to parliament and avoid a recurrence of a situation such as we have ait the moment.
I can only appeal to the common sense of the house in this matter; the government must follow the rules of parliament and the government wish to uphold the rules. It might be possible for the remainder of the present session to allow bills to pass second reading and to go to the committee as has been the case in the past, and for hon. members who wish to raise objections to particular bills, to raise those objections in the committee, it being understood that between now and next session the members of the government and other hon. members of the house will do what they can towards finding some means of freeing parliament from the necessity of continuing to deal with divorce bills along the lines which we have followed thus far.

Before the Prime
Minister takes his seat may I ask a question? It seems to me that the answer given is very satisfactory as far as it goes, but we must consider what we are to do for the remainder of this session. I have raised the objection that a number of hon, gentlemen are not competent to sit in judgment on these bills nor because of their religious convictions on this particular question are they competent to be members of the private bills committee. Would it be possible for us to follow the
precedent set by the senate, by which divorce bills are sent not to their private bills committee but to a special committee composed of those who have an open mind in regard to the question of divorce? I do not ask for an answer on this point to-day, but I would suggest to the Prime Minister that possibly this might be a way out even for this session. We might appoint a special committee composed of those who are not on principle committed one way or the other; that might relieve the pressure on the private bills committee and at the same time permit of greater impartiality in these matters than is possible under the present system.

I wish to say just a word in support of the attitude taken by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart). I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) has made himself absolutely ridiculous by his attitude on this question. The hon. member introduced a bill in this house, as was his right; that bill was defeated by the votes of hon. members who have an equal right to express their views. The hon. member was not a good enough sport to take his-
If the hon. member would speak a little louder I would be able to hear him.

I hope the hon. member will be equally pleased when he does hear what I have to say. I say that the hon. member was not even a good sport; he introduced a bill into this house, which he had a perfect right to do-

I rise to a point of order. It has not bean my conception of order in this house that personalities could be exchanged between one member and another in describing the action taken by a particular member.

I do not gather that the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Mc-Gi'bbon) has made any personal reference to an hon. member, but he falls .into another error; he is leferring to a past debate of this session.

It was not my intention to discuss the personality of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), or that of any other member in this house; I am simply discussing the attitude he has taken when, having been defeated on a certain bill, he still persists in blocking the business of the house. As one coming from the province of Ontario, and as one who voted

Procedure Respecting Divorce
against that divorce bill, I say, with the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart), that this debate is not- facilitating the purpose he has in view. When the province of Ontario asks for a divorce court then it will be time enough for this house to consider it.
I rise to a point of order. Is the hon. member in order in discussing a question which has been already disposed of by this house?
We have been discussing it for two weeks.	.
The hon. gentleman should confine his remarks to the present bill.

I do not know whether or not you are complimenting me, Mr. Speaker, when you restrict me within narrower limits than has been the case with other hon. members who have spoken on these bills. We in the province of Ontario are not going to be dictated to by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, either on this question or on any other. If he thinks he is going to gain his object by blocking the business of parliament in order to force upon the province of Ontario something which it has not as yet asked for, he is taking the wrong way to accomplish his ends.

Mr Speaker, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr Mackenzie King) has in a very few words this afternoon done much to eliminate the present source of trouble and pave the way to a serious and constructive settlement, not only of the bills which may come up this year, but of the whole question. I admit Mr. Speaker, that it has been psychologically impossible to discuss any one olf these bills without discussing what I call the basic principle of them all. The comment on rule 92 which was read a moment ago by the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. March), illustrates the whole system. The private legislation dealt with in paragraph 844 refers only to occasional private bills; but these hundreds of divorce bills arise from this fact, or principle of law, that matters have to be dealt with as private legislation, either by parliament or by the local legiMatures, according to the subject, when they cannot be dealt with properly by courts of judicature.
It has been made quite clear during the course of these debates that this method, call it obstruction if you like, is the most effective manner in which to bring to the consciousness of the house and of the country the importance of this question. This discussion has made at least one point clear in

the minds of many members of both houses- a point which had been quite obscure in the minds of the people of the country, and [DOT]certainly in the province of Quebec-that applications for divorce do not come to parliament merely and exclusively as petitions from certain individuals to obtain the redress of certain individual grievances. It has been amply demonstrated that petitions for divorce come before this parliament because, under our constitution*-as far as the provinces of Ontario and Quebec are concerned-this is the only legislative and judicial body which can deal with the question. I have endeavoured, without any spirit of antagonism or animosity toward anyone, to bring home to the minds of the hon. members of the house the fact that this question must be dealt with one of these days in a radical fashion.
Therefore, to that extent, I agree with the hon. member for Bonaventure; but in order to respond in a sympathetic spirit to the invitation of the right hon. the Prime Minister to all members of the house to present their views towards the satisfactory settlement of this important question, I must take exception to other comments which have been made by the hon. member for Bonaventure. The hon. member for Bonaventure has referred to the declarations made at the time of the Quebec resolution by Sir Hector Langevin when these very important questions of marriage and divorce were 'being discussed. I understood the hon. member for Bonaventure to take the same view as did Sir Hector Langevin, that jurisdiction respecting marriage and divorce had been confined to this parliament in order to prevent the extension of divorce to Ontario and Quebec which had not been afflicted with that plague. But Sir George Etienne Cartier and Sir Hector Langevin did not realize that in wishing to avoid one issue they simply raised a broader one. They did not consent to have divorce enacted for Ontario and Quebec, but they had divorce enacted for the whole of Canada including Ontario and Quebec. They forgot that basic principle of the constitution to which I referred the other day, and to which the hon. member for St. Lawrence-JSt. George (Mr. Gahasn) replied, " Well, it is elementary law": the moment you establish a principle of law you assume the moral obligation to supply the judicial mechanism to put it into practice. My point of view is that the parliament of Canada, having accepted the responsibility of legislating upon marriage and divorce for the whole of Canada including Ontario and Quebec, has left itself open to the receipt of petitions from any in-

Procedure Respecting Divorce
habitant of Ontario and Quebec. They can apply to this parliament for a divorce, parliament acting in its dual capacity of a legislative body and a court of justice.
That brings us back to the awkward position which was described by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth). If we are a court of law, then he is absolutely right when he says that my humble self, the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion), the hon. member for Bonaventure, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), and many others are prejudiced upon principle upon these questions. In fact, if we are imbued with the basic principles of our creed it is just as wrong for us to vote for any divorce law or any individual divorce bill, as it would be to vote for a bill of this- house similar to those introduced into the English parliament in the time of Elizabeth, or Edward VI, or Henry VIII, declaring that the practices of our religion were blasphemy. It would arouse the indignation, not only of every Catholic member, but of every fair-minded member of the house to put us back to the days of the sixteenth century and to ask parliament to place the stamp of blasphemy upon any article or creed of religion believed in by any hon. member. We have, thank Heaven! passed those days in every part of the British Empire.
I admit, I repeat, that we went for years without reflecting upon the basic issue contained in these bills, but now we are realizing it; and my purpose in raising these debates was simply to bring to the attention of hon. members that, believing as we do, we cannot go on doing what we have done for years .past, proclaiming to our people that we are opposed to the principle of divorce, and then letting pass every bill of divorce that comes before the house. It has been said that we ought not to vote for the principle of divorce, if contained in a bill transmitting from this parliament to another body, a court of justice, a jurisdiction granted to parliament by the constitution to be exercised in a judicial manner; in other words, that we cannot transfer to a court of justice those powers which we exercise, but that the principle of divorce is not contained in the three hundred bills before us. That opinion may be held by very respectable people in Quebec, including priests, but I do not think it is good teaching, good law or even good common sense.
Therefore in that spirit I suggest to the members of the government; in the same spirit I suggest to the leading men of the opposition, including and beginning with the 78S94-114
leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), who is undoubtedly one of the best legal minds of the country, that they approach this question with a spirit absolutely foreign to any thought of party gain or appeal to this province or that, to this creed or that. We will accomplish nothing if we approach the question from the point of view of party gain. There are in the house a large number of members representing millions of law-abiding citizens who are opposed to divorce on principle and who are horrified at the manner in which divorce has grown, just as there are other members who, in an equally respectable manner, one which would call for my respect if not for my adherence, would be horrified at the idea of the house adopting from year to year a series of measures that would, for example, prepare the way for the breaking of the British Empire. To me it would not appeal as much as it would to them, but I would respect their viewpoint. Therefore I think this question should be approached at the same .time from the viewpoint of those who are opposed to divorce and from that of those who, not being opposed to divorce, want divorce granted or refused according to some principle of law or practice and some respect for equity.
It has been suggested that if we amend the rules of parliament with respect to divorce bills, we could see, for example, that justice is done to the children; that something is done for the support of the innocent party and the children who may remain in the custody of the innocent party. But there [DOT]again you strike the rock of constitutional objection, because we cannot deal here with civil rights or property. We are entirely precluded from that. So that my humble contribution to the preparation of a remedy for the situation is to repeat what I said1 last week. Let us go to the root of the question and, finding that the whole problem of marriage and divorce is intimately connected with the matter of civil rights, with the matter of property; that already all the provinces of Canada have exclusive jurisdiction over the solemnization of marriage, let us come back to the spirit of the constitution and simplify the whole matter by handing the whole problem over to the provinces. This is the only way that we can get rid of the objections, and that we can at- the same time give satisfaction to Catholics and to Protestants, to believers in the principle and practice of divorce and to those who do not believe in it.



Procedure Respecting Divorce
Moreover, it is the only manner in which we can ascertain whether Ontario wants a divorce court or mot. Some say Ontario wants it; some say it does not. Without referring to any past debate I say to-day that I do not yet know. Personally I would be prepared to vote to-morrow for a court of divorce for the people of Ontario if they wanted it, but I have no evidence to that effect. But if we hand the matter over to the provinces, then the people of Ontario, through their legislature which deals with civil rights, with the solemnization of marriage, with property, will be able to take up the whole question of marriage and divorce and establish courts of adjudication to pass judgment upon those questions as upon other questions of civil rights and property. This is the best we can do, and it is the suggestion I offer. I am quite sure if the solution were taken up in a broad way by representatives of the various parties in the house, they would secure for it the agreement of an. overwhelming majority of the people of this country irrespective of creed, race and province, because it is the sensible solution, the solution in keeping with the constitution.
Moreover, a point which has not yet been understood, in the province of Quebec, at least, and which I want to emphasize now is this: that if courts of divorce, as Sir Hector Langevin pointed out and as the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) pointed out this afternoon, were established in the eastern provinces prior to confederation, the courts of divorce working at present in Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan were established by federal legislation. This was unknown to the people of Quebec until a few weeks ago. I have seen printed in works that are considered as classics in Quebec, the statement that the Dominion parliament should not start the precedent of establishing divorce courts because it had1 never done so before; that divorce courts existed in the seven provinces because those provinces established them. Therefore, a classical author whose work is used in several of the colleges in Quebec, ignored the fact that the divorce courts of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta existed only under the operation of two federal acts, one passed in 1886, if my memory serves me aright, establishing in Manitoba all English laws as had been in force on the 15th July, 1870, and the other passed, I think, two years afterwards, establishing also all English laws in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. The result was the introduction, under federal legis-
lation, of the divorce law of England of 1857 in those three provinces.
And what about the judicature? This is a most interesting point, which exemplifies the point I made last week, and which was immediately ratified, so to speak, by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-iSt. George (Mr. Cahan). When a divorce case was taken before the supreme court of Saskatchewan, the judge excused himself on the ground of having no jurisdiction. He said:	I see no statute
conferring jurisdiction upon me to adjudicate upon divorce. The question was taken to the privy council and the privy council, putting into force that long-standing principle of British jurisprudence, declared:	Where there
is a lawr there is a tribunal to adjudicate upon it; and since the federal parliament of Canada has thought proper to introduce all English laws, including the divorce law, in the province of Saskatchewan, there must be a court of law to adjudicate upon such issues, and the supreme court of Saskatchewan, which exercises the same jurisdiction as similar courts in other provinces or in England, is the tribunal to which every ratepayer of that province has the right to appeal. All those questions were absolutely unknown to the people of the province of Quebec, and I dare say to the people of the province of Ontario.
These debates, Mr. Speaker, have not been useless, let my hon. friends on all sides admit. They have been raised, not for the pleasure of obstructing legislation or playing upon the nerves of anybody, but so far at least as I am concerned, and I think in this matter I can speak for my hon. friends on the other side, with the sincere object of finding a solution for one of the most important problems of government, of legislation and of public order. These days have not been lost, these debates have not been in vain, and if the Prime Minister, with the help of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), after consultation with the members of this house and with enlightened men from the province of Quebec and the province of Ontario can find a solution for this great problem, they may be assured that after some years have passed, it will be looked upon as one of the most important achievements of this parliament. It will have been a greater service done to the country than the passing of many of the appropriations and administrative bills which this house spends many hours discussing eveiy session. I do not say this in any spirit of disparagement of hon. members who take more interest in other questions, but simply because in my opinion this is a more important problem.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, to put a practical conclusion to these remarks, I may say that

Private Bills
for this session I am prepared to let pass on division the second reading of these bills. I do not promise to let them pass through the committee and receive their third reading without pointing out some discrepancies in the evidence, but I admit at once-as this question was put to me the other day by the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Boys)-that the question of evidence, so far as I am concerned, is entirely subordinate to the question of principle. I consent to let this procedure go on for this year because, as the Prime Minister says, a question of this nature, with all its complexities, cannot be settled at once. Indeed, if the Prime Minister had suggested that he was prepared to settle it this week, I would have taken advantage of my years and have advised him to make haste slowly because this is an important matter. At the same time I request from him, as a Canadian citizen, more so than as a member of parliament, and I request also of his colleagues, and of the members of the . opposition, and of every member of this house, that they give sincere and serious consideration to this problem and be prepared to make to the house whatever constructive suggestions they may have, so that we may bring to this vexed question a solution that will be as much in harmony as possible with the requirements of the various provinces and of Canada at large.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PROCEDURE RESUMING ON THURSDAY OR FRIDAY DEBATE ON AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Last year the mernbel
for Victoria, B.C., when a motion was made that I should leave the chair for the house t-o go into committee of supply, moved an amendment thereto on the dumping duties, if I remember well. The debate went on until the house ajourned. The next day was Thursday and automatically I did leave the chair when the motion was made to go into supply. Then later on the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Anderson) rose to address the house, two or three days afterwards, on the 10th of May, I think. Prior to that as (Objection was taken that the debate had lapsed, I quoted what May says, page 476:
If an adjourned debate on such an amendment is standing upon the order paper when supply, for consideration of which in committee it is not necessary to propose the question for the Speaker's leaving the chair, is to be taken, the order of the day for resuming the adjourned debate is removed, and procedure on the amendment lapses, in order that the Speaker, in obedience to standing order 28 may leave the chair without question put.
Last year my ruling was that if the procedure had lapsed the question itself did not lapse. A question which has been decided by the house is a judgment of the house and it cannot be revived during that session. But when as in that particular instance the procedure lapses it does not follow that the question itself lapses and it can be revived. Here is what May says at page 234, 12th edition:
When an order of the day has been read, the proceedings thereon may be cut short by the adjournment of the house whilst those proceedings are in course of transaction, or before their resumption, when they have been postponed at a quarter past eight o'clock. An order of the day, in such cases or if, when the order is read, no day is appointed for its future consideration, drops off the notice paper, as the house has made no order thereon.
That is the case in the present instance.
In committee the same result may be produced, either by a failure of a quorum of the house, or by a resolution directing the chairman to leave the chair. To replace a dropped order of the day upon the notice paper, a motion is made (before the commencement, or after the close, of public business, to appoint the order for a subsequent day. These motions, which are made without notice, are usually treated as purely formal motions.
In the British system of parliamentary government the greatest latitude is given in regard to freedom of speech and the discussion of public matters, and when a question accidentally lapses by some definite rule that question may be revived. It is a dropped order, as May says, and it can be revived. In the present instance the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart), having given due notice to revive his lapsed motion is perfectly in order in taking it up to-day. Last year- and I speak from memory-the motion was not made by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Anderson), but as far as I remember there was an agreement between both sides of the house that the question should come to an issue and the hon. member simply continued the debate.
I therefore rule that the present motion is in order; the superseded debate can be revived, subject of course to the decision of the house.

That was one of the reasons which influenced us last year in adopting the practice suggested by Your Honour, instead of reviving it by a substantive motion, as perhaps the Prime Minister will recall, in order that no question might arise with respect to the fact that the Speaker had automatically left the chair in the meantime and it would seem senseless to move an amendment which would prevent him from leaving the chair when he had already left it. speechtext:
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved the second reading of Bill No. 130, to amend the Canadian National Railways Act.

He said: As I explained in response to a question when the bill was introduced, it seeks to make a number of minor amendments to the Canadian National Railways Act, amendments which are made necessary by references which were rather mixed up in the revision of the statutes but which will become clear to anyone reading the sections which are designed to correct the errors. There is, however, one important provision which is contained in section 2 of the bill. It can be dealt with probably more intelligently in committee of the whole than at this stage of the bill. Briefly, it seeks to make available to the Canadian National Railways the provisions of the Expropriation Act, and as it will be of some interest to my legal friends in the house, I can say that the object of it is to endeavour to secure a uniform procedure in connection with large matters of expropriation which, from the point of view of the Canadian National, can be more conveniently carried on through the exchequer court, than by the means available in various parts of the country. As is well known, the exchequer court can, in minor cases, delegate to a district court or other judge an investigation, but by this amendment it will be possible, in large cases, to make available the machinery of the exchequer court. In looking over the debates at the time when the Canadian National Railways Act was originally passed, I gather that there was then a very substantial desire to make available that machinery, but the matter was not pressed and the ordinary provisions of the Railway Act were made available. After looking into the matter with some degree of thoroughness, I am of opinion that, as regards large expropriations such as are sometimes involved in matters connected, for instance, with the Montreal terminals and so forth, the exchequer court is better machinery than would otherwise be available. For the information of the house I may say that such expropriations as have taken place in Montreal recently have been taken under the Government Railways Act by the minister in order to make available the provisions of the exchequer court procedure instead of the ordinary procedure which would be available in such cases. I would suggest that all these various features can be better dealt with in the committee stage of the bill.

At any rate, we have

this government passed the order in council under that statute, without the statute the order in council was impossible, so at least-

Without the act there

Yes, the system, but no consolidation of it. The system existed in the statute, but the railways were not consolidated until the order in council was passed. The hon. gentleman may say that he is the stepfather of the enterprise, but the father was the statute passed in 1920.
There is one thing I have to say about the use of the exchequer court. It works a great injustice against people in a small way in life, who are really unable to grapple with the situation. This session I have received several letters amongst them one this morning which I received from British Columbia in connection with the expropriation by the government of property near North Vancouver for a rifle range. The exchequer court took proceedings and arrived at certain conclusions. These people were told that they could have $75 for a lot of land which cost them, with taxes since they bought it, several hundred dollars. They say:	We are wholly incapable financially of embarking in exchequer court litigation. The provisions of the old Railway Act enabled one right in the community, with the aid of a district court judge, to carry on these proceedings, and it could be done without the aid of a solicitor at all. Frequently the owner himself presented his case, brought in his witnesses, and had it disposed of. Certainly I have known very great injustice to be done where people are placed in a position such as contemplated by this bill. I agree entirely with what the minister has said with respect to large matters in a city like Montreal, for instance, but might it not be desirable to say, "Where the sum tendered by the government for the land taken does not exceed" so many dollars,, so as to make clear the question of juridiction. I am only throwing out this suggestion at the moment for the *consideration of the minister, because on the second reading of the bill I am not going to take up the time of the house needlessly, but when it comes back to the house I should like to discuss that phase, having regard to

Simcoe Post-mastership-Mr. Bennett
the cases that have been brought to my attention recently in connection with the Vancouver rifle range, where if the information that I have received is correct, considerable hardship has been done to the owners of property in that locality.

Motion agreed to, and bill read the second time.
