By unanimous consent the house resumed from Wednesday, April 17, consideration of the proposed motion of Mr. Robb for supply, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Stewart (Leeds):
That all the words after the word "that" in the motion he struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"In the opinion of this house the Postmaster Ganeral has acted in a most arbitrary manner and in utter disregard of the letter and the spirit of the Civil Service Act in connection with the recent appointment of a postmaster at the town of Simcoe."

['Mr. Speaker, I have received from the Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs a message issued by His Majesty the King from Craigwell House today. I think hon. members would be interested in hearing it, and if the house will give me permission I will, notwithstanding that we are past the hour of adjournment, read the message. It is as follows:
In looking back on my long illness and recovery my heart is full of thankfulness of far deeper origin than any mere sense of relief.
I have been brought back from danger and weariness of the past months by the wonder-full skill and devotion of my doctors, surgeons and nurses. And help has come from another source of strength:	as month after month
went by I learned of the widespread and loving solicitude with which The Queen and 1 were surrounded. I was able to picture to myself the crowds of friends waiting and watching at my gate and to think of still greater numbers of those who in every part of the empire were remembering me with prayers and good wishes. The realization of this has been among the most vivid experiences of my life.
It was an encouragement beyond description to feel that my constant and earnest desire had been granted-the desire to gain the confidence and affection of my people. My thoughts have carried me even further than this. I cannot dwell upon the generous sympathy shown to me by unknown friends in many other countries without a new and moving hope. I long to believe it possible that experiences such as mine may soon appear no longer exceptional: when the national anxiety of all the peoples of the world shall be felt as a common source of human sympathy and a common claim on human friendship.
I am not yet able to bear the strain of a public ceremony but I look forward on some appointed day to joining with my people at home 
and overseas in thanking Almighty God not merely for my own recovery but for the new evidence of a growing kindly significance of the true nature of men and nations.
In the meantime I hope this message may reach all those even in the remotest corners of the world from whom I have received words of sympathy and goodwill.
(Signed) George R. I.']

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition) :
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock last Wednesday I was directing attention to the fact that under the provisions of the Civil Service Act any objection to a particular candidate named by the Civil Service Commission must come from the deputy minister, not from the minister himself. That fact was referred to by the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) in one of his public addresses. But, as he said the other day, he was prepared-as indeed he must be under our institutions-to accept responsibility for the actions of his deputy. I merely say that to close the matter with which I was then dealing.
But before I proceed more particularly with the resolution introduced by my hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Stewart) I desire to point out that in Le Droit, under date of April 20, 1929, an article appears in which it is alleged that the attack against the Postmaster General is being made virtually because he happens to be of French origin. Mr. Speaker, I desire to say how strongly we resent such a statement in the public press of this country A free translation of the article-which I will not read in full lest it should empty the house -would be this in part:

These attacks need hardly surprise us since Mr. Veniot himself has done all he could to provoke them. It is a crime for certain people to see that constitution is respected, to see that the two official languages are on a footing of equality, and that the field of action of the French language is extended a little. We do not fear to say that certain people object to the father of the bilingual postage stamp more than to the minister who is charged with favouritism.
Could anything be more injurious to the peace and happiness of the commonwealth, could anything be more subversive of the unity of this Dominion than the publication of an article of this character-it is signed by Charles Gautier-in which it is asserted that the minister because he is the father of the bilingual postage stamp is being attacked in this house, when as a matter of fact the true reason for our criticism is his inefficiency in the conduct of his department. This is another passage from the same article:
All this noise (about certain appointments or dismissals is like .a tempest in a teapot; it is the madness of fanaticism against a minister who is convinced that the sun shines for everybody, and acts accordingly. A minister who, bke Mr. Yeniot, tries to put in practice the letter as well as the spirit of the constitution deserves the support of all political and national elements.
Those of us who recall a report of a speech by the Postmaster General that appeared in the public press of Montreal-in regard to which the hon. minister stated that he had been inaccurately reported-find here a reflection of exactly what was said on that occasion. Here is an appeal being made once more to racial origin and to political predilections, the kind of appeals of which the Postmaster General is a past master, and we resent with all the Strength of which we are capable this editorial allegation that the effort on the part of the opposition to bring to the attention of the Canadian people the gross inefficiency that at the present time characterizes the conduct of the Post Office department is in any sense influenced by the fact that the minister happens to be of Freneh-Acadian origin. It would make no difference to us from what race he is sprung. We are not dealing with the man, we are not dealing with his racial origin, we are not dealing with his religion; we are dealing with the Postmaster General, with the man who has been entrusted by the Canadian people, through the Prime Minister, with the conduct of a greait department of the government, and if in the conduct of that department it becomes necessary for those who sit to the left of the Speaker to draw attention to the gross inefficiency of his administration,

Simcoe Postmastership-Mr. Bennett
we shall resent, such a construction being put upon our criticism, and we shall ask the Canadian people for their judgment as to whether this sort of thing which has been going on for the last ten years is to be continued, whether our efforts to bring about the correction of abuses and maladministration are to be frustrated at every turn by an appeal to the bilingual issue. It is time that such appeals be frowned upon, it is time that some more effective answer was made to the charges directed against the hon. gentleman's inefficient administration of his department.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there is an amendment to the motion to go into committee of supply which deals with the case of the appointment of a postmaster at Simcoe. With thait I propose briefly to deal, for it is now apparent not only from the number of cases which have been brought forward in this house, but from the letters which every member to your left is receiving as to what is happening in his district, now that attention has been focussed upon the Postmaster General's department, that a general motion only will satisfy the people in this regard. It is no longer the Simcoe post office; it is every post office w'here the minister has had an opportunity at the behest of Liberal members to exercise political patronage in this department of the public service.
Let me for a moment draw the attention of the house to the fact that in the effort to promote a decent public service and bring it under the control of the Civil Service Commission many, many difficulties were experienced. Those difficulties were raised not any more by the Liberal party than by the Conservative party. But it was fortunate that at the particular moment the Union government was in power and found it possible to place upon the statute books legislation that enabled us to have a civil sendee so far as possible free from politics. What was the purpose of the Civil Service Act? The purpose, first of all, was to promote efficiency in the public service and, secondly, to assure continuity in office so long as the civil servant did not interfere in the politics of the country, and thereby give a dignity to the service of the crown that had been denied in days gone by.
I repeat what I said the other day, that at the election of 1911 a very large number of the public servants believed that because the Liberal party had been in power so long they were perfectly within their rights in taking an active part in the elections of that year. They did take an active part, and they
paid the price by being removed from office.
I well recall the circumstances under which Mr.-now Sir Robert-Borden's government passed an order in council providing that if members of the House of Commons would certify over their signatures that given individuals in their communities had been offensive partisans at the election, they should be removed from office. I also recall that the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier approved of the general terms of that order. Action was taken accordingly, and when last session the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) was able to stand up in this house and say of his own knowledge that he believed a given person to have been guilty of political partisanship, you will recollect, sir, that at once I said the incident was ended so far as we were concerned. He was absolutely within the order in council, and the postmaster who he said, of his own knowledge, had been guilty of offensive partisanship undoubtedly must have expected to be relieved from office. Why? Because it has always been contended, before the Civil Service Act was passed at all, that any servant of the crown who saw fit to take part in elections publicly must be prepared to yield up his position if the fortunes of war went against him. The Right Hon. Mr. Fielding, former Minister of Finance, laid down a principle

I do not know that I can repeat the exact words-that any person appointed to a public position, as a servant of the crown, must first of all discharge his duties as such. He was not thereby debarred from taking an interest in public affiairs, or to exercise his franchise if he so desired, but he must not interfere actively in the politics of the country, for, by so doing he ceased to be a servant of the public.
This Civil Service Act with all its defects, as we all must realize, was made possible in its present form when a union government was in power. It is the duty of all of us, whether we sit on the right or the left of the Speaker, or whether we constitute a group of lesser numbers than those who sit directly to the right or to the left, to assist, in my judgment, in promoting the efficiency of that act. It should be maintained in all its power and efficiency, and no government in power to-day -and they may not be to-morrow, meaning by to-morrow some future time-would dare say that the act should be repealed. This act should not be tampered with, and that is why we as a party are taking the strong stand that we are taking to-day. It was held by the privy council many years ago, in a case that came up from Australia-and the member from Marquette (Mr. Glen) will remember
1808	COMMONS
Simcoe Postmastership-Mr. Bennett
it-that no public servant could be dismissed from office without cause being assigned and a reason given, to enable him to defend himself and his reputation from all that is involved in being dismissed from office without an opportunity to be heard. Only the other day you will recall that General Booth was removed from office by the high council of the Salvation Army. An injunction was applied for and granted by Mr. Justice Eve. Why ? Because it is an elementary rule of our law that a man who occupies a position such as he did must not be removed from office unless he has had an opportunity to be heard, and has been given the reasons for which it is proposed to dismiss him. Mr. Justice Eve granted the injunction.
I recall, as I stand here, the case of an Indian agent dismissed by order in council, and he does not know to this day why he was removed. But I also recall, too, that Mr. -now Sir Robert-Borden laid down the rule that no man should be removed from office without having an opportunity to defend himself against the charges laid against him.
Many of the cases that were read the other day by the Postmaster General are cases in which men were active partisans. They had to be removed from office because of that. I recall two cases in the city in which I live, one of them, I believe, a collector of customs, the other occupying a position in the land office. Both tendered their resignations immediately after the election, because they had gone out and taken an active part in the election. The postmasters named by the Postmaster General the other day were dismissed because they had taken an active part in the election. Any man who went out and took an active part in the elections of 1925 and 1926, whether he be a Liberal or a Conservative, must have known at least the consequence of his own act. He must now expect the consequences and give up the office which he holds, because he has seen fit to participate actively in a political campaign rather than give his service to the state in the way in which I have indicated.
Now, look what has happened in this country. For sixteen months, from October to February, the Postmaster General on an average has dismissed one postmaster a day. That is the return to this parliament. That is his record, one a day. And what is more, Sir, let us turn to his record in connection with the Civil Service Act; take the Department of Justice, the Department of Trade and Commerce, the Department of Finance; take any of the other departments and compare the number of cases in which the Civil Service IMr. Bennett.]
Act has been overridden with the number of times it has been overridden by the Postmaster General. You had the figures given you the other day. Practically as many as all the other departments put together. The Postmaster General has seen fit to overrule the Civil Service Act of this country to that extent. Was that accident? Does anyone think that all those men were dismissed, as mere accidents?
And that brings me to this case from Simcoe. I dealt with the facts the other day, and now it would seem to me the situation is simply this: a vacancy; applications for the appointment; a decision by the Civil Service Commission; a rejection by the deputy minister. And then you ask: was that rejection warranted on any ground of high public policy, or by the statute itself? And, unless you can affirmatively answer that question then indeed you fail. If the Postmaster General, through his deputy, rejected, without warrant, then on the ground of high public policy-meaning by that the efficiency of the post office service -this motion is warranted and it should be adopted by this house.
What are the facts? Without going into them in further detail to-night, it is only necessary to point out that, first of all, you have an amputation case. You have a case in which the disabled soldier was a soldier who had suffered the loss of both his limbs below the knees, one below the ankle and the other between the ankle and the knee. The amputation cases are not easily taken care of in this country. It is not easy to re-establish the amputation case. It is not easy to provide positions in the public service for those who have suffered an amputation of both legs. There are a limited number of positions which they can fill. They are very limited in number. In some instances they are able to operate elevators with but one arm, or with one leg. You find them doing work of that kind. But there is a limitation upon the work that they can do, and that is the reason, I take it, that the statute provided for a preference being given to the disabled soldier over the ordinary case of the returned man. His disability gave h:m a preference over his fellow, the man who fought side by side with him, the man who came out of the war whole in body while he came out with his legs gone, or his arms gone, or suffered a disability recognized by pension. He then receives at the hands of the law, under the statutes of this country, a preference over the man who came out of the war whole. This man had a preference given to him by law, and the Civil Service Commission in reckoning that preference gave him the posi-

Simcoe Postmastership-Mr. Bennett
tion. And why? We have it that Doctor Roche and Mr. Tremblay both saw the applicant. They realized that he was fit to discharge the duties of postmaster at Simcoe. The Postmaster General says "I say he is not. This man could not handle mail bags, could not do the work that I think he should be able to do". And yet that excuse was not brought up until long after he had been awarded the office by the action of the Civil Service Commission itself. Was it warranted? Is there any question but that there was political interference which brought about this situation? Is there any doubt about it? In making his defence the other evening the Postmaster General referred to certain things which took place at the meeting in Simcoe.
I hold in my hand a copy of the Simcoe Reformer of October 18, 1928, a Liberal paper-
Some hon. MEMBERS : No.
It is independent.

I confess that I am not
in a position to state with any degree of authority; I assumed it to be a Liberal paper from its name, but names do not always correctly interpret political opinions. The other evening the Postmaster General said that Mr. Whittaker seemed rather convinced by the story told by the Postmaster General in his speech at Simcoe. According to this paper Mr. Whittaker is quoted as follows:
If Mr. Veniot is correctly reported, w'hat he says absolutely untrue. His motive for attributing these statements to me is very clear, in that such a declaration on my part would absolve Mr. Veniot and his followers from all suspicion of patronage in my case. I had not intended to say anything more for publication about my side of the question, but in view of this absolute fabrication I feel compelled to make public what actually happened in this regard from the beginning, and to expose certain untruths contained in Mr. Veniot's address at Simcoe.
Last summer, after word of the appointment of Mr. Bowyer to the postmasterShip had come through. I was approached by a member of the local Liberal executive, presumably delegated by W. H. Taylor, M.P., the Liberal member for Norfolk, and was offered a proposition somewhat as follows: The local Liberals, hacked by the member, were to agree to lend me their support in securing an appointment at Brantford, Ont. In return I wias to promise to maintain a discreet silence in regard to my treatment at the hands of the Postmaster General and not to he seen conversing in public with any person known to be of the Conservative stripe. In addition, I was to be bound by the conditions of a letter which they were to submit for my signature and which was to be made public prior to the public announcement of my appointment. The purport of this letter was to the effect: (1) That I had no grievance against .the local Liberal member or any of his
followers. (2) That I was now satisfied that I would not have been physically able to handle the position of Postmaster at Simcoe. (3) That I felt duly grateful to the postal department for their foresight in refusing to allow me, in spite of myself, to assume a position the duties of which they considered, in the kindness of their hearts, to be far to onerous for a man in my position.
After due consideration of the principles and ethics involved in this proposition, I, as an ex-soldier of His Majesty's forces, could not bring myself to be a party to a dishonourable scheme of this kind. Consequently my answer to their plan of barter could only he a fiat refusal.
Nothing further happened in regard to the purchase of my silence until the evening before Mr. Veniot's meeting in Simcoe. It was the night of October 3, when my friend Sam Morris of Port Dover, also an amputation case, was approached by A. A. Winter. K.C.S, of Simcoe. They were attending a meeting in Port Dover in connection with proposed improvements to the harbour, at which Hon. J. C. Elliott, Minister of Public Works, was present. In the course of their conversation, Mr. Winter stated that the local Liberal party were prepared to secure for me any job which I would be able to handle, and at this time suggested that Mr. Morris get in touch with me and arrange an interview with the government party the following night in Simcoe to discuss the possibility of finding me a position.
Accordingly the interview was arranged through Mr. Morris, but for some reason Mr. AVinter dropped out, and we went to Mr. A7cniot's meeting with no definite appointment in prospect. At the conclusion of the meeting, Mr. Morris accompanied me to the platform, where we secured the attention of Mr. Taylor. M.P.. who at once brought up my refusal of the Brantford proposition. I reiterated my stand in this regard. He then expressed his willingness to remove the conditons of acceptance referred to above, since he admitted being resposible for having them attached to the proposal.
It was at this time that Mr. Veniot approached us, and after shaking hands with us, as a matter of course, he stated that he would help me get the position. He remarked that I was not to consider the post office episode a personal matter and that he bore me no hard feelings. This was all that was said between us, and, after shaking hands again, Mr. Veniot bade me good-bye.
The statement which he attributes to me as having been uttered at this meeting constitutes an absolute falsehood and a deliberate attempt to lead the public astray, as well as a contemptible effort to justify bis position by shifting for onus for his high-handed conduct from his own shoulders.
Before departing, Mr. Taylor said that we would have a talk about the matter of the Brantford position. Ten days have elapsed and I have heard nothing more about it. In any event I couild not conscientiously .become a party to such an arrangement, .which savors of the same political patronage as has permeated the entire case. I wash my hands entirely of all dealings with the men who, in my heart, I believe have been guilty of the basest treachery to a man who fought for his country and sacrificed both limbs on the fields of France.
1810	COMMONS
Simcoe Postmastership-Mr. Bennett
I will not read the rest of the article, which is a discussion of what took place at Simcoe; I am not concerned with that at the moment. This is the statement made by Mr. Whittaker in reply to the remarks of the Postmaster General. We all remember the kind of letter the Postmaster General1 wrote in connection with another case, in which he left out the important facts. Asked wrhy he did not state those facts os they were; asked why he was willing to write something which he knew to be untrue he said he did not desire to hurt anyone's feelings. What confidence can we place in the word of a minister who writes such a letter as that? I put that question to this house, and- there are hundreds of people throughout Canada to-night asking the same thing, men and women who have read the debate, men and women who hold small offices as postmasters and postmistresses throughout our rural communities; they are asking themselves that question to-night just as I am putting it to you. Heretofore it always has been the rule that when we had such a letter as was produced the other evening over the signature of a minister of the crown, we could rely upon it as representing the facts, but we now have a minister of the crown saying it was not true, that he knew it was not true and that he wrote the letter in that way for some purpose other than the real reason appearing on its face. I say that conduct such as that does merit the disapproval of the Canadian people through their representatives in this parliament.
1 have not had an opportunity to look up the records, but some effort has been made in that direction in order to see if there ever was another case such as that, and so far as I have been able to find out there never was another. There it is. Some of my hon. friends who have followed the debates in other countries will remember that in one case in England a minister of the crown was peremptorily dismissed by his Prime Minister because there appeared to foe some suspicion of a lack of frankness on his part. Hon. .members may recall that within the last few years one minister of the crown resigned his office, great though it was, because of some suspicion attaching to the attitude he had taken with respect to a public matter, and those who have followed affairs in India will recall that a prime minister dismissed from office a minister of the crown who had given a letter to the public under circumstances which raised some suspicion as to the bona fides under which it bad been done. We in Canada sometimes follow a looser practice and allow ourselves to be deluded by outside considerations. With

the facts as stated I have no hesitation in asserting that Mr. Whittaker would have been postmaster of Simcoe to-night if some one had not interfered for political reasons.
Let us see what that interference was. There is the statute-not the regulation-which says that the applicant must be a bona fide resident of the locality; that was read to this house the other afternoon and I will not read it again. Mr. Bowyer did not reside nearer to Simcoe than two miles from Hamilton. He was assessed on a piece of property in Simcoe, but his letter clearly indicates that in his opinion he at least was not residing in Simcoe at that time. There is the statute; the inspector found him at Mount Albion; the other gentleman sent out to investigate found him there also. Therefore I say we have no satisfactory answer to the question which hon. gentlemen are asking themselves in this house: Was the rejection warranted? That is the question which must be answered; everything else sinks into insignificance. Stripping this case of everything else we have just one question to answer: "Was the rejection of Mr. Whittaker warranted?"' Everything was regular up to that point; the vacancy, the advertisement, the application, the investigation, the appointment to office as far as the Civil Service Commission could do it, the report that he was physically fit, the inspection, the visit to Ottawa !by the applicant and the rejection by the Deputy Postmaster General, who, you will recall, the other day in another case which was dealt with by the Postmaster General pointed out that he took a certain action because the minister told him to do so. That is part of the record. As I say, we have the rejection by the Deputy Postmaster General, and the only question this house can ask is very simple. It is this: Was that rejection warranted? When the members of this house vote upon this motion they vote yea or nay to that quetion, "Was the rejection warranted''? Was the Postmaster General warranted in rejecting this young man who had suffered: two amputations and who walked up and down the corridors of this building, parading himself before the Postmaster General in order to demonstrate his ability to walk without the aid of a cane. He sold his business to obtain the better job. He points out that he was receiving a pension for his disability; he was within that favoured, ultrapreferred class. I ask the members of the house, sitting as judges, whether that rejection was warranted? Is there one of us who is free from political bias who would say that upon those facts the rejection was warranted? That

Simcoe Postmastership-Mr. Bennett
is what we must vote upon; that is what the issue is; that is what this amendment to the resolution to go into supply means.
When we find the public journals endeavouring to inflame the public mind by making the appeal to forty per cent of the population of this country that the attack upon the Postmaster General is being made because he is of French origin, we say that that is an insult to the house, and we on this side of the house will continue to do our duty. We make that answer to this and all similar cases. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) can make some other answer to his constituents in Regina and elsewhere, but we will stand for evenhanded justice for every man and woman in this country regardless of race or religion.
The hon. gentleman's followers in Saskatchewan are now going in the directly opposite direction.

I am glad the hon. minister said that, because the only report I ever saw was the report of a public speech made by the Premier, Mr. Gardiner, himself in Saskatchewan and to which I directed the minister's attention last year.
I shall be glad to send my hon. friend a copy.

I shall be glad to see it.
As the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) is now in his seat I would ask him to define to the house, in order that it may not be said in the remote sections of the constituencies of this country that appeals are being made to racial animosities and prejudices, what the constitutional rights of the French and English are under the constitution with respect to bilingualism. I ask him to define that so that there will be no misunderstanding. It is the duty of the Attorney General of Canada to do that.
The article in Le Droit says that the Postmaster General is being attacked because he is the father of the bilingual postage stamp. Before supply is granted I want the Minister of Justice to define the constitutional rights of minorities and majorities, and then it will be seen that there never has been a departure by the Conservative party from those rights as established by the constitution. It will be remembered by those who know the political history of this country that the Conservative party, because of a judgment of the privy council defining the rights of minorities, went down to defeat and almost suffered extinction at the hands of the electorate. Those are the facts, and it is time that this sort of thing was discontinued, that efforts to make political capital out of such statements in the by-ways and hedges of the remote sections of the country be stopped.
When the Minister of Justice and the Attorney General of Canada has defined what the position is in law; when he has defined the constitutional rights with respect to bilingual postage stamps and other matters of that kind, then he will find that no voice has been raised against the enjoyment to the full of the rights of all men and women under the constitution, be they majorities or minorities. The old red herring has been dragged across the trail-the old effort at which hon. gentlemen opposite are past masters; the effort which has served them so well in days gone by but which will not continue to serve them again. The record will be placed upon Hansard to show that there is no doubt that there has never been a time when this has been the case. It has been said within the shadow of parliament that an attack is being made on the Postmaster General for one purpose only, and in the discharge of our constitutional duty we must point out these facts.
This is a very serious matter to those of us who have been endeavouring as best we can during the last year to keep down such agitations to stop them whenever we have seen them, and to endeavour to promote unity, harmony, respect and regard for the constitutional rights of all peoples in this country. When a statement like this appears in the public press and is allowed to go uncontradicted it is taken as being admitted, and gathers force and strength as it travels along.
But that is not an answer to the question. Was the rejection warranted? I have heard no words from the Postmaster General which would establish before a responsible judge or jury the fact that it was warranted. It is upon that question that we will presently vote. This resolution is limited to the Simcoe post office, but there are many other eases which will be dealt with before supply is granted to the Post Office Department. We will vote upon this resolution and presently upon a general resolution, in the public interest, and which touches the administration of the post office, declaring that the utter disregard of the Civil Service Act, and gross partisanship in dismissals to the extent of one per day for sixteen months by the Postmaster General merits the condemnation of this housse.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. C. ELLIOTT (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I desire to
refer to some of the remarks made by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat

Simcoe Postmastership-Mr. Elliott
(Mr. Bennett). I hope he will pardon me if I think that .the greater portion of his remarks have perhaps no bearing whatever upon the resolution, which is now before the house.
He made a statement at the beginning of his remarks with regard to the censure which should be placed upon a certain newspaper for saying something which did not have a tendency to promote harmony and unity among the peoples of this country. I am going to leave it to the house and to the country as to whether the remarks with which the hon. gentleman prefaced his address would have the tendency of promoting harmony and unity among the peoples of this country.
Because my time is limited I desire to refer first to what the hon. gentleman said in his remarks the other evening. I read his statement with a good deal of care, and I must say in this connection that I am not interested in making a defence of the Postmaster General (Mr. Yeniot), because, in my humble opinion, Canada has never had, among the excellent postmasters general who have presided over the department, a gentleman who has conducted the affairs of that department with greater efficiency and with more regard for public service than my colleague the present Postmaster General has done and is doing to-day. I feel that I should make some reference to the remarks made the other evening by the hon. gentleman when he referred to my hon. friend the member for Norfolk-Elgin (Mr. Taylor), and said that he was going to show his connection with this particular matter. I will read what he said: It appears at page 1671 of Hansard:
But the Civil Service Commission had no knowledge of it.
That was the question of Mr. Bowyer's entitlement.
The minister said he had; and why did the minister intervene? Is not this the fact? The member for that riding, as I shall presently show-
And as he never did show.
-and the Liberal organization in that county, said, "We must interfere and get this job for Bowyer." That is the record, as I shall show in a moment.
I followed his remarks the other evening and I listened with great attention to his remarks to-night with some expectation that he would carry out the promise he then made to show that the hon. member for Norfolk-Elgin or somebody else had interfered in the matter so as to enable Mr. Bowyer to get this position. But though he made that promise, which apparently came so readily to him at the time he was making those remarks, neither in his subsequent remarks the other evening nor in
	1
his remarks to-night has he said one word that would by any possibility connect the hon. member for Norfolk-Elgin with endeavouring to obtain this appointment for Mr. Bowyer as is suggested in that paragraph.
I read what Mr. Whittaker said.

My hon. friend knows perfectly well that he made a suggestion that he was going to prove what he said, and he carried on with that flourish of trumpets which is so peculiarly his own. But he took great care never to get back to it again during the whole course of his speech.

Then the hon. member
could not have been listening.
Why did he not get back to it? Because evidently he has read the record and he knows that from one end of it to the other there is not the slightest vestige of evidence to bear out that statement.
It was on the minister's personal file, I suppose.
Whatever file it is on, my hon. friend promised to prove it and he did not do so.

I read what Whittaker
said.
Let us just consider this. What are the facts?
Excuse me. I regret I interrupted the minister and I shall not do so again.

I will try to keep to the facts in connection with what the record shows. I have only forty minutes, but I do not object to interruptions as long as they do not take too much time.
Let us consider the facts. It is only fair to the returned soldier who has not obtained the position, that all the efforts and misrepresentations that may be made from any side of this house shall not prejudice him. Let us get clearly into our minds first of all that this is not a contest between a Liberal and a Conservative. Both applicants were Liberals.
One was an official Liberal. The other was not.

I do not know exactly what my hon. friend means by an official Liberal or an official Conservative, but I know what an artificial Conservative is. In order that there may be no question in regard to the matter, may I call attention to the gentlemen

Simcoe Postmastership-Mr. Elliott
who recommended Mr. Whittaker. First of all the file shows that he was recommended by Doctor W. A. McIntosh. Anybody who knows anything about the county of Norfolk-Elgin and the town of Simcoe knows that Doctor McIntosh is one of the most influential Liberals in the town of Simcoe, a former president of the Liberal Association and a prospective candidate in that riding in the 1926 election in the Liberal interests.
The next recommendation comes from Mr. Groff, manager of the Bank of Montreal, not an active politician but a man who is known to be a prominent Liberal in the town of Simcoe. Next comes George Williamson, whose letter shows that he was in favour of Whittaker and at the time of writing the letter, dated the 22nd February, 1927, addressed to the chairman of the Civil Service Commission, Mr. George WTlliamson was president of the Liberal Association of the town of Simcoe. Also in the editorial of the Globe newspaper of the 6th October, 1928, it is shown that this young man voted for Sir Wilfrid Laurier in the general election of 1917, and it shows perfectly clearly that, although he was a disabled returned soldier at that time, he was a very enthusiastic Liberal. That is the question with regard to politics, and I cannot understand why, in view of those facts which my hon. friends must know, they would endeavour to argue that the matter is a political one.
What is the next point? I must get it clearly into the minds of every hon. member and everyone in the country that this is not a contest between a returned soldier and a civilian for this office. It is a contest between two returned soldiers, and, if I may say so, two of the most gallant young returned soldiers who were privileged to come back from France and Flanders, because they both served in the war with distinction and with great credit to their country. It is true that Bowyer had to give a wrong name in order to get his enlistment because he was very much under age, being only a little over sixteen. Mr. Whittaker was a little over seventeen. Both enlisted before they were of military age. Unfortunately Whittaker was in France for only eight months when he suffered a very severe injury resulting in the loss of both feet and making him what is known as a double amputation case. The other boy remained in France for, I think, two years, fighting for his country with great gallantry. He came back with honours and medals. Therefore, in that respect the men are equal.
Then comes the question referred to by my hon. friend as to the disability. One man, Whittaker, had a total disability-and this is something that I refer to with some hesitation, but I think the facts should be clearly before the house before we vote on this motion-and he was obtaining the pension that is given to a man who is 100 per cent disability.	.

So much more to his
credit.
I was not asking my hon. friend for that suggestion, and I do not know that it is helpful in the discussion. If, however, he insists, I have no objection.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Except that it is taking up my hon. friend's time.

Yes. That is the situation. Very shortly afterwards, in 1918, Whittaker was taken on the staff of the Soldiers Settlement Board. For nearly six years he had a position with that board, receiving somewhere around $1,800 to $2,200 a year.

Which was coming to him,
which he received as remuneration for his services.

Surely nobody would suggest that any department of this government would pay anything that was not coming to anyone. He earned it. He was hired and he received that salary. He received it, of course, in addition to his pension, making between $3,400 and $3,500 that he was drawing altogether. He thought that he could better himself by taking a position which he was offered with a jam company in Simcoe, where he received a somewhat smaller salary, perhaps a little less than he was getting with the Soldiers Settlement Board; but he was at home and naturally, I suppose, the expenses were a little less.
I want to follow Mr. Whittaker's statement just a little further because my hon. friend was good enough to refer to the fact that something took place at some meeting at which I was present. The meeting to which he refers took place in the town of Port Dover. I will just read the clause which he read, and then leave it to the judgment of the house to say what was the impression they received from that statement. He said:
Nothing further happened in regard to the purchase of my silence until the evening before Mr. Veniot's meeting in Simcoe. It was the night of October 3, when my friend Sam MoTris of Port Dover, also an amputation case, was approached by A. A. Winter, K.C., of Simcoe. They were attending a meeting in Port Dover

1814	COMMONS
Simcoe Postmastership-Mr. Elliott
in connection with proposed improvements to the harbour, at which Hon. J. C. Elliott, Minister of Public Works, was present. In the course of their conversation Mr. Winter stated that the local Liberal party were prepared to secure for me any job which I would be able to handle, and at this time suggested that Mr. Winter get in touch with me and arrange an interview with the government party the following night in Simcoe to discuss the possibility of finding me a position.
I do not want to do this young man an injustice but I leave it to the judgment of the house to say if the reasonable inference from that statement was not that these discussions took place at the meeting which I attended, and I want to say positively that no such discussion took place in my presence. I see that my hon. friend disclaims any intention to convey that impression. If so, I accept his intimation. Nothing whatever was said at the meeting I attended with regard to Whittaker obtaining a position or anything of that kind, and I say that whoever drafted that statement did not at all events successfully make it very clear that that was what he intended to convey.
Certain things 'have been said by him and read by my hon. friend with regard to false statements being made by the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot). I want to refer to certain statements that were made by Mr. Whittaker, and I leave it to the house to judge. Mr. Whittaker made an affidavit, and in his statement he says-I do not know just what to think of this, but it appears in the Globe of the 15th of October:
As a matter of fact I had owned the business only four months and naturally had not a chance to discover if it were a profitable business. I would never have made any declaration about it if the Civil Service Commission had not advised me that if I wished to show that I was properly re-established

I think he means "not" properly reestablished.
-it would be necessary for me to take an affidavit to the effect that my business was not paying. Mr. Veniot has now used this affidavit as an instrument to prove that I lost nothing by selling my business. I can only say that if I had not received my notice of appointment as postmaster I still would be the owner of that business, and I am sure that I could have made a success of it.
Hear, hear.

Perhaps my hon. friend
who is so ready with his "hears, hears", will listen to the kind of success this man said, in his affidavit, dated April, 24t'h, 1928. He states:
(1)	In February, 1928, I purchased a monumental stone business believing it to present an opportunity for successful re-establishment.

(2)	That I had only a layman's knowledge of said business.
(3)	That since entering this business I have steadily depleted my financial resources without any adequate return.
(4)	That my experience during the past three months indicates that competition in this business is so keen as to force me either to seek more capital in order to carry on or wind up affairs.
(5)	That I see no prospects of securing more capital and I shall be obliged on this account to relinquish said 'business at a considerable loss.
There you have his affidavit that he could not carry on the business unless he could get more capital, that he saw no prospects of getting more capital, and he must relinquish the business at a considerable loss. Then you have his statement later that he is sure that if he had retained the business he would have made a success of it. All I have to say is that those are his statements, and the house can take them for just what they are worth.
Something has been said with regard to the duties which the postmaster had to perform. Some suggestions have been made by hon. members that the duties of the office were changed after the applications were in, making the duties more onerous than they were formerly, and making the office a class 2B, which it was not before. Perhaps I should give to the house just what was said in that regard. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) says at page 1657 of Hansard:
And the classification was changed after the application was made.
Mr. Veniot:	No. The hon. gentleman is not
stating the exact truth. I do not mean that offensively at all.
I know he would not. Then the hon. member for Vancouver Centre goes on:
But the Postmaster General will admit that the change to class 2B took place after the application was made.
That shows that my hon. friend, who always wants to be fair, while desiring to be fair, at least has a most suspicious mind. I just took the trouble to look the point up. The dismissal of Lawson took place on the 15th of January, 1927. The chief superintendent of the post office service on that date issued this letter to the district superintendent at London:
The district superintendent is informed that the Postmaster General has authorized the removal from office of Mr. I. D. Lawson, postmaster at Simcoe, in view of incompetency. The office is to be placed for the present under the temporary charge of Mr. Charles E. Kaid, of Simcoe, the transfer to date from the 1st of February, and concurrent with the temporary transfer, the office is to be changed to the grade 2B basis.

Simcoe Postmastership-Mr. Elliott
That was on the 15th of January, the date of dismissal of the former postmaster, and one month and two days before the advertisements were issued asking for applicants to fill the position that had been vaeated. That decides to a certain extent, when it becomes a class 2B office, what the salary is to be. The minimum salary is $2,040 per annum with annual increases of $120, and the advertisement that went out was in accord with that understanding. It also stated that the applicants must be either natural born or naturalized British subjects and residents of Canada for three years, and must possess the ability to perform efficiently the duties of the office. After all,
I submit that that is the real test of the kind of postmaster they were trying to get-he must be a postmaster who could efficiently perform the duties of the office.
Next the suggestion was made by my hon. friend, but it was not pressed in his remarks, and so I shall pass over it very briefly, that Bowyer was not a resident of Simcoe. It is quite apparent that when the inspector first went out to make his inspection, Bowyer and his wife were on one of Bowyer's father's farms near Hamilton. Bowyer apparently had not been reestablished to anything like the same extent that Whittaker had been. He reported that Bowyer was not a resident of Simcoe. Now, I appeal to my hon. friend's fairness, if the member for the riding, the Postmaster General, the Deputy Postmaster General and the inspector were trying to make out a case to have Bowyer appointed, would it have been reasonable for the report to have been sent in as it was that Bowyer was resident outside the locality and in the vicinity of Hamilton.

They cannot give the
inspector all the instructions.

And he cannot have all
the wisdom. The inspector gets pretty definite instructions. If my hon. friend will look at the book of instructions issued to each inspector he will find that he has to make these examinations, bearing in mind the class of duties that are to be performed, the amount of mail to be handled, the distance it has to be taken, the number of rural routes to be served, and the handling of the mail bags.
<Mr. ARTHUR'S: Will the hon. minister lay a copy of those instructions on the table?

I am sure the Postmaster
General will accommodate my hon. friend.
Will it be done?

If my hon. friend wishes
it.
Yes.

They are public property. My hon. friend will understand that these are all departmental regulations. I wondered whether my hon. friend's suspicions with regard to residence and to the grade of the post office being changed arose from a naturally suspicious mind, so I obtained the voters' list for the town of Simcoe. It is based on the assessment that was made before applications were called for. I find at page 74 Bowyer's name and his wife's appear as tenants. The fact of the matter is that his father had several farms in the vicinity, and this boy, wffio perhaps was not quite as efficient as he had been before he went overseas, worked for his father on several of the farms, and his explanation at the time the inspector made his inspection was that he and his wife were during the summer visiting at a farm in the vicinity of Hamilton. The finding is that he was all the time a resident of the town of Simcoe. So I think perhaps that disposes of the question of residence.
Next we come to the question of how these appointments are made, what is required. It will be found that as far back as 1918 an arrangement was made between the Civil Service Commission and the postal department as to appointments to the postal service. On account of the necessity of appointing officials who would be able to perform the duties, which duties were better known to the postal department than to the Civil Service Commission or anybody else, the postal inspectors were to pass upon these various applicants. That is the practice which has been followed since that time. In that connection may I call the attention of the house to the statement made by the chairman of the commission, Doctor Roche, to Mr. Williamson, in a letter of February 24, 1927:
No doubt you are acquainted with the procedure in filling such positions. The position is locally advertised by the department, applications to be sent in to the district superintendent of the postal service, London. This officer will despatch one of his inspectors-
That is, the district superintendent of postal service at London, will despatch one of his inspectors.
-to Simcoe on a certain date to interview the applicants, and it largely depends upon the report of the inspector and district superintendent as to who receives the appointment.
In a letter dated February 26,	1927,
addressed to Colonel Parkinson, who was then Deputy Minister of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment, Doctor Roche made a similar statement. He said:
The commission however largely depends upon the report of the post office inspector and
1816	COMMONS
Simcoe Postmastership-Mr. Elliott
district superintendent of postal service, who, after interviewing all the applicants, place them in order of merit from the post office standpoint.
And another similar letter appears at page 107 of the file, written to Mr. Beverly Anderson, who had interested himself on behalf of either Mr. Whittaker or Mr. Collver, in which it is stated:
It will largely depend upon the nature of that officer's report as to who will secure the position.
That was the practice, and it was followed in compliance with the regulations. I have the letters here, but as my time is short I will not trouble the house to read them. One is dated February 22, 1918-shortly after the act came into force-and is from Mr. Foran, secretary of the Civil Service Commission, to Doctor Coulter, the answer being dated February 26, 1918. These brought about the arrangement by which the local postal in-pectors were to make the examination of the applicants. A postal service inspector did make that examination and reported thereon. The same applies to Mr. Bowyer. In a letter of March 10, 1927, Mr. Foran, secretary of the commission, writing to the superintendent of the postal service at London, says:
Mr. Bowyer is being advised that his application has been transferred to you for the necessary report on his qualifications.
I think the house perhaps has not received from my hon. friend from Leeds or from my hon. friend the leader of the opposition as clear an impression as is desirable that these examinations are not made by the Civil Service Commission's inspectors, but by the inspectors of the postal department.
Now, what is the report? When the report comes in the man placed first on the list is John Alexander Wallace. He had no previous postal experience. He represented Norfolk county in the Dominion parliament from 1921 to 1925, and he served on the board of governors of Toronto university and of the Toronto General Hospital. I think he was the Progressive member for the riding at that time, and I do not believe you could find a man better qualified to make a good postmaster. However, he was a civilian and was passed over. From the standpoint of political advantage to the member, I have no doubt that that would have been the most advantageous appointment to make. He was evidently a man of prominence in the community, but his case never was pressed. The next man reported on was Charles Rex Bowyer. This is the report of the examiner:
[Mr. Elliott.)
Charles Rex Bowyer is a married man, 28 years of age. Has a good education. Resided at Simcoe until about a year ago, but is now living at Mount Albion. Has had no postal experience, but would devote his entire time to the work. Was a student previous to enlistment and since discharge has been farm manager for his father, W. A. Bowyer, and is engaged in looking after some seven or eight farms owned 'by his father. This applicant states that owing to his being a minor he enlisted under an assumed name, that of C. R. Musgrove, and served twentyjseven months in France with the R.C.H.A. Discharged by reason of demobilization. No physical disability. Is a fine type and impressed me favourably.
The next man is Donald Smith. Then there is the name of Grover C. Murdock. He was not a returned man. He is the next on the list, and Whittaker was only seventh on the list. So that if Bowyer had not been appointed, in all probability one of the other returned men would have come in next instead of Whittaker.
Well, the examination was made, and the report reached the Civil Service Commission in due time. But on account of the difficulty in identifying Bowyer with Musgrove-because that was the name under which he enlisted as he was under age-some considerable time was taken in making sure that he was the same man, and, on February 18, 1928, Mr. Foran, the secretary, addressed this letter to the Deputy Postmaster General. I will just read the last paragraph because it is No. 32 on the file, and the whole letter appears on the file:
I should be glad, therefore, if the department could furnish the commissioners with a definite report, at as early a date as possible, with reference to Mr. Whittaker's physical fitness for this poetmastership.
The report comes in a little later, and is dated 5th March, 1928, and is as follows:
When questioned, Mr. Whittaker stated that it would be impossible for him to do any heavy lifting.
If the Simcoe poet office were a revenue office, the postmaster could, if necessary, hire an additional clerk to perform the heavy work and in the case of a city office, there would be sufficient other work so that it would be necessary for the postmaster to perform duties of a heavy nature, but, in the case of a 2B office, it is my opinion that what is required is a working postmaster.
His appointment, therefore, would probably make it necessary to add an additional employee to the 2B Simcoe post office.
I find my time passing pretty rapidly, but I want to call attention to this: The notice was issued. Now, what I say is this, that the judgment that w'as being relied upon by the Civil Service Commission, in making this ap-

Simcoe Postmastership-Mr. Hepburn
pointment, was the judgment of the inspector from London who reported that Whittaker was unable to perform these duties, and you will note-if my hon. friends will be good enough to look at the appointment dated May 29, 1928-that it contains this clause which, I venture to say, will not be found in many notices if in any other; it certainly is not in the appointment when Mr. Bowyer was notified:
(Appointment subject to physical fitness.)
It also calls attention to the fact that:
The deputy head may at any time before the expiration of six months reject any person assigned or appointed to any position under his control or direction, or he may extend the period of probation within which such person may be rejected for another six months; and the cause of rejection, or the reason for extending the period of probation, shall be reported by the deputy head to the commission.
And the ruling of the Department of Justice dated the 9th December, 1919-and I think this is very important; it is on the bottom of the notice that was sent-
Sent to whom?

To Whittaker. The ruling reads:
If the deputy be reasonably satisfied upon preliminary examination of the person nominated that the latter is unsuitable or not qualified for the duties of the office or employment to which he is assigned, I think he may, if he think it advisable, reject him without entrusting him with the discharge of any duties; otherwise in conceivable cases considerable prejudice to the public service might ensue.
Will the minister permit a question?
Order.
Was Whittaker given an opportunity to show what physical fitness he had to carry on?

I was just hoping that
would be the question my hon. friend would ask: Was Whittaker given an opportunity to show what fitness he had to carry on? My contention, Mr. Speaker, is that in view of the report of the inspector who, by arrangement between the Civil Service Commission and the post office, is the inspector upon whose judgment the Civil Service Commission must depend, he never was appointed. What would be the sense, I would ask my hon. friends-
He was recommended by the Civil Service Commission.

I would ask, what would be the sense in giving him a trial? What would
be the sense in giving a trial to a man who had been reported -by the competent official as being quite incapable of performing the duties of the office to which he was about to be appointed?
Answer the question.

Why would you take a
man who was reported by the inspector as being incapable of performing the duties and give him a six months' period of probation?
I am now going to come to what I think is a complete answer to this resolution. What does the act say? The act says, section 24:
The deputy head may, at any time before the expiration of six months, reject any person assigned or appointed to any position under his control or direction, or he may extend the period of probation within which such person may be rejected for another six months; and the cause of rejection, or the reason for extending the period of probation, shall be reported by the deputy head of the commission.
Whittaker had been appointed subject to probation.

Oh no. My hon. friend
has not, I am afraid, been paying the attention which he usually pays. He had been appointed subject to a certificate of physical fitness, and no certificate of physical fitness had ever been made to the inspector who is the judge as to physical fitness, and who reported that he was physically unfit.
Now, I also want to call attention to this-
Time.
I beg the hon. gentlemen to kindly listen to the hon. member.

I want to say I would not object to the question, only the time is very short, and I had hoped that my hon. friends during this discussion would get into their heads what really took place in connection with this matter.
I referred to the question of rejection. I want-
The hon. member's time has expired.	*

In my observations in this house I have always been impressed with several things which emanate from the other side of the house. One is that on every possible occasion my hon. friends hug the old flag to their bosoms, raising shouts of patriotism. Another is how, when they find some unfortunate individual, they can depict most terrible conditions and pose as the champions of such an unfortunate.
ISIS	COMMONS
Simcoe Postmastership-Mr. Hepburn
I refer to the famous McConachie case in Halifax. In the present case hon. gentlemen opposite are taking advantage of the infirmities of a poor unfortunate soldier in order to make political capital. The expression has been coined to-night that we might differentiate between an official Liberal and an official Conservative; some further reference was made to an artificial Conservative, and I would particularly refer that expression to hon. gentlemen opposite if they are really sincere in their desire to look alter the interests of returned men. I would ask them to turn their attention to the provincial government of Ontario, and in this connection I am going to refer to just one town, the town of Simcoe, whose post office is under discussion now. I find that since 1926 the provincial government has appointed many men in that town; they appointed the clerk of the surrogate court, a civilian and a Tory; the issuer of motor licenses and the examiner for motor licenses, civilians and Tories; the entire staff of the liquor store, all Tories and all civilians with one exception. Those appointments were made during the time my good friend from Fort William (Mr. Manion) was on the Liquor Control Board. I do not know just what effort he made to curb the greatest exponent of patronage in this country, Hon. G. Howard Ferguson, or whether he made any effort. I would also point out that just recently the jailer of the town of Simcoe resigned and according to the Brantford Expositor his successor has been named already in the person of George M. Bough-nee, a civilian and a defeated Tory candidate in that riding.
Now I want to tell hon. gentlemen opposite that they are not humbugging the people of Ontario at all by putting their feet in one direction and their face in another with regard to the returned men, their duplicity is so apparent that they are not going to get by with it. My riding adjoins the county of Norfolk, in which county this controversy has arisen, and I want to assure the Postmaster General that he has nothing whatever to fear with regard to these unfair attacks. I say that Mr. Whittaker, a poor unfortunate soldier, has been caught in the whirlwind of this Tory barrage, and is finding himself left with so many public utterances which are not true and according to fact that I believe he is sadder and wiser for having been a tool in the hands of hon. gentlemen opposite.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) read certain extracts from the Toronto Globe with regard to a statement made by Whittaker in which he said an attempt had been

made to buy his silence. In order to refresh the memory of the house I will read just what Mr. Whittaker said:
Last summer, after word of the appointment of Mr. Bowyer to the postmastership had come through. I was approached by a member of the local Liberal executive, presumably delegated by W- H. Taylor, M.P.. the Liberal member for Norfolk, and was offered a proposition somewhat as follows: The local Liberals, backed by the member, were to agree to lend me their support in securing an appointment at Brantford, Ontario.
